messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Computing global encounter rate
parts:
Florian:

Encounter rate only makes sense at the stratum level, which is why
Distance does not show it to you at the global level if you have
performed a stratified analysis. If you did not presume that encounter
rate varied across your study area then you likely would not have
stratified your analysis. If you would like to know the global
encounter rate, I think you could simply run your analysis without
stratification. I'm not saying you should use the density/abundance
estimate produced therefrom, but if you have curiosity about the global
encounter rate, you can obtain that statistic by performing your
analysis without stratification.

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Computing global encounter rate
parts:
Adding to what Eric said, it depends on the reason why you want a global
rate. I've not come across an example where it is a sensible thing to
calculate, but it is easy to calculate. Eric's suggestion of ignoring
stratification is the simple solution, and effectively weights by line
length in each stratum. Depending on the purpose, you might prefer to
weight by stratum area. You can get this by taking a weighted average
of the stratum encounter rates, with weights proportional to area.
Because encounter rate is independently estimated in each stratum, there
are no covariances, so finding the variance of the weighted average is
straightforward - evaluate weight squared times variance of e.r. for
each stratum, then sum these. Take square root for std error, and
divide by the average encounter rate for cv. (This assumes weights are
normalised, so they sum to one.)

Steve Buckland
